messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Chinedu's Silence

Chinedu was nineteen when he was taken. The abduction happened on a Tuesday evening in March, outside the community center where he'd been working a part-time security detail. Three men forced him into a van. For seventy-two hours he was held in a basement—a space without windows, lit only by a bare bulb that never turned off. His captors' voices came at him in Pidgin and broken English, layered with the sound of a generator that ran continuously, a mechanical thrumming that seemed to vibrate through the concrete walls. They demanded information he didn't have, asked questions that made no sense, and when he couldn't answer, they used their fists. The darkness, the noise, the helplessness—all of it pressed into him like a physical weight. When the police found him, he was dehydrated, bruised across his ribs and face, and nearly silent.

His parents brought him home to their apartment in Newark. Within a month, Chinedu had enrolled in the police academy's accelerated program, determined to reclaim some sense of control, to become someone who could never be made helpless again. By eighteen he was in uniform. At nineteen, he was fast-tracked to detective work. His superiors saw ambition and resilience. What they didn't see was the man who couldn't sleep, who had begun to construct an increasingly rigid architecture of avoidance to keep the memories at bay.

The memories themselves were the problem. When they surfaced—unbidden, at his desk or during interviews—Chinedu found himself trapped in a peculiar kind of paralysis. He knew what had happened to him with absolute clarity, could recall the sequence of events, the physical sensations, the fear. But when he tried to speak about it, even to his girlfriend Amara or to the department psychologist, the words simply dissolved. His mouth would open and nothing would come. Not because he was being evasive, but because the experience seemed to exist in a register beyond language, something that his voice couldn't reach or shape. This inability to articulate what had happened fed directly into his need to suppress it entirely. If he couldn't put it into words, perhaps he could put it out of his mind altogether. He began, consciously and methodically, to refuse to think about the basement, about the generator's hum, about the men's voices. He would catch himself starting to remember and would clamp down hard, redirecting his attention to case files, to the next interview, to anything in the present moment.

The suppression required vigilance. It required him to avoid situations where memory might intrude. Nighttime became dangerous—the darkness seemed to invite the basement back, to make the generator sound return in his ears. He stopped going out after sunset. He declined invitations from colleagues for evening patrols, made excuses to Amara about why he couldn't walk with her to the late movie. His world contracted into daylight hours and brightly lit indoor spaces. At work, this became noticeable. He was passed over for a stakeout assignment because he'd refused night shifts without explanation. His captain asked if everything was okay. Chinedu said it was.

The suppression also meant physical distance. Touch had become dangerous—not because he feared being hurt, but because physical contact could trigger the memories he was working so hard to keep buried. When Amara reached for his hand, he would find a reason to pull away, to adjust his collar or check his phone. When his mother hugged him, he would stiffen, his body refusing the comfort even as some part of him ached for it. She had begun to cry quietly when he left the house. He knew this was hurting her, hurting his relationship, but the alternative—allowing someone close enough to touch him, to potentially trigger the cascade of suppressed memory and sensation—felt impossible. The emotional intensity of the trauma would sometimes break through anyway, arriving without image or context, a wave of terror and rage that left him shaking in the bathroom at the precinct with no clear memory of what had triggered it.

By his second month as a detective, Chinedu was isolated in a way that felt both protective and suffocating. He came to his first therapy appointment because Amara had given him an ultimatum, and because he was beginning to suspect that the architecture he'd built to keep the memories out was becoming the very thing that was keeping him trapped.
